Sow once in early spring, be patient (parsnip is slow to come up and needs fresh seed each year), and let the roots size up all summer. Wait to dig until after a few fall frosts, since cold weather sweetens the flavor, and you can keep harvesting right through a mild Piedmont or Coastal Plain winter.
parsnip.region_notes_seasoned: No Virginia Cooperative Extension or NC State planting table lists parsnip for the Mid-Atlantic; this cell instead mirrors parsnip's own cold-climate long-season calendar (documented for the northern tier) shifted to this belt's earlier frost dates, since parsnip's slow, months-long root development and frost-sweetened flavor are not tied to any one climate band. Sow once in early spring; the crop then grows through summer with no sowing or harvest activity to exclude, and is dug from fall into winter, holding well in the ground behind this belt's comparatively mild z7/z8 winter.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Garlic overwinters dormant, resumes growth in spring, and bulbs mature in early-to-mid summer as the lower leaves brown; the warmer Coastal Plain (zone 8) finishes first, the cooler Piedmont (zone 7) a couple of weeks later.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest window closes by midsummer; garlic left too long past maturity has its wrapper split and stores poorly.

8.zone_notes: Coastal Plain and Piedmont warm edge: set cloves mid-October into mid-November so they root before the ground cools, overwinter under a light mulch, and dig bulbs from late May into late June once the lower leaves brown. Both hardneck and softneck types do well here.

7.zone_notes: Piedmont: set cloves in October so they root before hard freeze, mulch once the ground starts to cool, and dig bulbs from mid-June into mid-July. Hardneck types (Rocambole, Porcelain, Purple Stripe) reward the belt's real winter chill with scapes and rich flavor; softnecks succeed too.

garlic.region_notes_beginner: In the Piedmont and Coastal Plain, plant garlic in fall, October into mid-November, not in spring. The cloves grow roots, then rest through winter under a layer of straw or leaves, and finish the following summer. Dig the bulbs in early-to-mid summer once the lower leaves have turned brown, and let them cure in a warm, airy spot before storing.
garlic.region_notes_seasoned: Garlic in the Mid-Atlantic is a single fall-planted, overwintering crop, no spring planting: Virginia Cooperative Extension's 426-331 tables carry only a fall window for this crop (Oct 15 to Nov 15 in zone 8, Oct 1 to Oct 30 in zone 7), the belt's real winter cold serving as the vernalization hardneck garlic needs. Set cloves so they root before the ground cools, mulch once true cold sets in, and let the planting go dormant. Growth resumes in spring and bulbs mature in early-to-mid summer as the lower leaves brown, the warmer Coastal Plain finishing a little ahead of the cooler Piedmont; lift, cure, and store before the wrappers split from over-maturity.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set onion sets or seedlings per Virginia Cooperative Extension's zone 8 Onion (bulbing) table (Feb 20 to Apr 20), the belt's single spring window; VCE carries no fall column for onion here, and onion is cold-hardy enough to go in well before the last frost. Zone 7 runs about a week and a half later.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Bulbing is triggered by day length, not by days since planting, so the harvest window is anchored to the last frost rather than to the planting date: bulbs size up as days lengthen and mature when about half the tops fall over, roughly mid-to-late summer regardless of exactly when sets went in.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The pull window closes at the slow end of maturity, after which bulbs are lifted and cured two to four weeks before storage.

plantings_provenance.basis: Built from VCE 426-331's zone 7/zone 8 Onion (bulbing) spring rows (no fall column carried for onion in this table); harvest timing anchored to last_frost rather than to plant_out, since bulbing is a day-length trigger, mirroring this crop's own established modeling method for a photoperiod-gated crop.

8.zone_notes: Coastal Plain and Piedmont warm edge: set onion sets or seedlings Feb 20 to Apr 20 as soon as the soil is workable, well ahead of the last frost since onion tolerates cold. Bulbs size up through early summer and pull late June into late July, near the southern edge of long-day territory, so intermediate-day types are a strong alternative here.
8.day_length_note_seasoned: This belt sits at the warm edge of long-day onion country (roughly 35 to 36°N in the Coastal Plain). Long-day onions bulb here at 14 to 16 hours of daylight, which the belt's summer provides, but choose a fast-maturing long-day variety since the growing season is on the shorter side for the type. Intermediate-day onions (12 to 14 hours) also bulb well at this latitude and are a strong, well-suited alternative; avoid true short-day (Southern) types, which are bred for fall planting and mild winters this belt does not reliably offer.
8.day_length_note_beginner: Long-day onions are the safe choice here, though this zone sits close to the line where intermediate-day onions work just as well. Long-day onions wait for the long days of summer before making a bulb; pick a quick-maturing variety since summer here is a bit shorter than the true North. Intermediate-day onions are a good alternative too. Skip short-day (Southern) onions, which are meant for fall planting in places with much milder winters.

7.zone_notes: Piedmont: set onion sets or seedlings Mar 1 to May 1 as soon as the ground can be worked. Bulbs size up and pull late June into late July. This latitude (roughly 37 to 40°N) is squarely long-day onion territory, though intermediate-day types also perform well near the belt's southern edge.
7.day_length_note_seasoned: This latitude (roughly 37 to 40°N, the Virginia, Maryland, and Pennsylvania Piedmont) calls for long-day onions, which bulb at 14 to 16 hours of daylight, well matched to the belt's summer day length. Intermediate-day types also perform here and are a reasonable hedge for the belt's warmer southern edge; avoid true short-day (Southern) types, which need a fall planting and a mild winter this belt does not reliably provide.
7.day_length_note_beginner: Grow long-day onions here. They wait for very long summer days (14 to 16 hours) before forming a bulb, which is exactly what this latitude provides. Intermediate-day onions are a reasonable alternative too, especially toward the belt's warmer southern edge. Skip short-day (Southern) onions, which need fall planting and a much milder winter.

onion.region_notes_beginner: In the Piedmont and Coastal Plain, onions are a one-time spring crop. Grow long-day onions (intermediate-day types work well too, especially in the warmer south of the belt). Set sets or seedlings out as soon as the ground can be worked in late winter to spring; onions shrug off a light frost. They are ready mid-to-late summer when about half the tops flop over and dry. Pull them, then let them cure in a warm, airy spot for two to four weeks before storing.
onion.region_notes_seasoned: Onion in the Mid-Atlantic is a single spring-planted crop: Virginia Cooperative Extension's 426-331 tables carry only a spring window (Feb 20 to Apr 20 in zone 8, Mar 1 to May 1 in zone 7), no fall column. This latitude spans long-day onion territory in the cooler Piedmont north (zone 7) to the warm edge of long-day, where intermediate-day types are an equally strong choice, in the Coastal Plain south (zone 8); avoid true short-day (Southern) types, which need fall planting and a milder winter than this belt reliably offers. Set sets or seedlings out as soon as the soil is workable, well ahead of the last frost since onion is cold-hardy. Bulbing is triggered by day length rather than by planting date, so bulbs mature on roughly the same midsummer calendar regardless of exactly when they went in; lift and cure two to four weeks before storage.

shallot.region_notes_beginner: In the Piedmont and Coastal Plain, shallots are a one-time spring crop grown from sets. There is no local planting guide specific to shallot, so this follows the same timing as onion, a very close relative: push sets into workable soil in late winter to spring, pointy end up, 6 to 8 inches apart. Each set splits into a clump you dig in early-to-mid summer once the tops flop over.
shallot.region_notes_seasoned: No VCE 426-331 row exists for shallot in this belt, so this cell follows the guide's Onion (bulbing) row, the closest related allium it documents, with an identical set-planted, spring-only culture and days-to-maturity range. Push sets into workable soil as soon as the ground allows, 6 to 8 inches apart, tip at the surface. The belt spans long-day shallot territory in the cooler Piedmont north to the warm edge of long-day, where intermediate-day seed hybrids are an equally reasonable choice, in the Coastal Plain south. The clump divides and sizes up as days lengthen, then is dug once most tops fall, roughly mid-to-late summer regardless of the exact planting date.

plantings.label: spring transplant, long standing crop, fall/winter harvest

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start seed indoors about 10 weeks before the transplant date, the lead this slow-growing crop needs to reach transplant size.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set transplants per Virginia Cooperative Extension's zone 8 Leeks (T) table (Mar 1 to Apr 1); zone 7 runs about three weeks later (Mar 20 to Apr 20). VCE carries no fall column for leek, consistent with a long-season standing crop planted once in spring.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Leeks reach usable size in roughly 90 to 150 days but are commonly left to grow on through summer and dug as a standing crop from fall onward, the belt's real fall/winter leek season.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Leek is genuinely winter-hardy: hardy maincrop varieties stand through fall and light freezes roughly zone 7 and warmer per this crop's own winter-hardiness model, a zone milder under mulch, so the harvest tail runs well into winter in this belt, longer in zone 8 than at zone 7's borderline edge.

plantings_provenance.basis: Built from VCE 426-331's zone 7/zone 8 Leeks (T) spring transplant rows (no fall column; a long-season standing crop planted once). A genuine overwintering-style harvest tail is authored per leek's own crop-level winter_hardiness model (hardy maincrop types viable roughly zone 7 and warmer, milder under mulch): zone 8 comfortably qualifies and carries the longer harvest tail; zone 7 sits at the model's own borderline edge and carries a shorter tail, with mulch called out in the notes.

8.zone_notes: Coastal Plain and Piedmont warm edge: start seed indoors in late December, set transplants Mar 1 to Apr 1, and grow the standing crop on through summer. This zone sits comfortably within leek's own hardy-maincrop overwintering range, so the bed is genuinely harvestable from September clear through January, with a brief quiet spell in February before spring transplants go in.

7.zone_notes: Piedmont: start seed indoors early January, set transplants Mar 20 to Apr 20, and grow the standing crop through summer. This zone sits at the borderline edge of leek's own hardy-maincrop overwintering range, roughly zone 7 and warmer, so the harvest runs a genuine fall-into-winter season through December; a heavy mulch pushes it further and is worth the extra insurance here.

leek.region_notes_beginner: In the Piedmont and Coastal Plain, leeks are a one-time, long-season crop that shines in fall and winter. Start seeds indoors in winter because leeks grow slowly, then set the young plants out in spring, once in early March to early April on the Coastal Plain or a few weeks later in the Piedmont. Grow them on all summer with steady water, then start digging in September. Leeks stand right through frost, even tasting sweeter for it, so you can keep harvesting fresh through fall and, where winters are milder, into the following winter with a thick mulch.
leek.region_notes_seasoned: Leek in the Mid-Atlantic follows Virginia Cooperative Extension's 426-331 spring transplant windows (Mar 1 to Apr 1 in zone 8, Mar 20 to Apr 20 in zone 7); VCE carries no fall column, consistent with leek's long-season, planted-once-per-year habit. Start seed indoors about 10 weeks ahead, since leeks are slow from seed, then set transplants out per the belt's own window. The standing crop grows on through summer and is dug from September onward: this crop's own winter-hardiness model rates hardy maincrop varieties (Lancelot, Large American Flag, Tadorna) viable roughly zone 7 and warmer, a zone milder under mulch. Zone 8's Coastal Plain and Piedmont warm edge sits comfortably inside that range, so the harvest genuinely runs from September into the following January; zone 7 sits at the model's own borderline edge, so its harvest is authored through December, with a heavy mulch a worthwhile hedge to push it further into winter.

direct_sow.label: fall
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: The fall sowing resumes once the worst summer heat breaks, timed to reach usable size well before the belt's first frost; scallion tolerates a light frost so the harvest tail runs a few weeks past it.

plantings.plantings_note_seasoned: Sow a short row every two to three weeks across each window for a continuous supply of young green stems; skip sowing through the declared summer heat exclusion.

This cell adapts the crop's own established multi-season, succession-eligible shape (used identically in this crop's northern_tier and se_gulf regions) to the Mid-Atlantic's real frost dates and its genuinely hot, humid summer (the belt is closer to se_gulf's climate than to the cool-summer North, per the region's own authoring rules), carrying a real, sourced summer heat exclusion rather than the cool-region's continuous window.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer heat exclusion (July): in the hottest month scallion seed germinates poorly in hot, dry soil and struggles to establish, and the green tops turn tough and sharply pungent, so sowing pauses through peak summer and resumes once it breaks. Not a frost gap but a heat exclusion. (Clemson HGIC; University of Maryland Extension)

7.notes: No VCE row exists for spring onion (scallion); windows follow this crop's own established multi-region succession pattern, shifted to the belt's frost dates.
7.zone_notes: Piedmont: sow Mar 1 to Apr 20 for a spring crop, then again Jul 10 to Aug 20 for a fall crop that runs to the end of October; the spring harvest bridges naturally into the fall sowing with no real idle gap, so no heat exclusion is declared here.

spring-onion.region_notes_beginner: Scallions are not in Virginia's own planting guide, so this follows the same pattern used for this crop elsewhere: quick and easy, harvested young and green, so bulbing and day length never come into play. In the Piedmont and Coastal Plain, sow in spring, take a break through the hottest stretch of summer (the ground is simply too hot for good germination then, at least in the Coastal Plain), then sow again for a fall crop that runs into late fall. Sow a short row every couple of weeks for a steady supply.
spring-onion.region_notes_seasoned: No VCE row exists for spring onion (scallion) in this belt; this cell adapts the crop's own established multi-region succession pattern (University of Minnesota Extension; Clemson HGIC; University of Maryland Extension) to the Mid-Atlantic's real frost dates and its genuinely hot, humid summer. Sow in spring, then again in late summer for a fall crop that runs into late fall; scallion tolerates a light frost. In the Coastal Plain and Piedmont warm edge (zone 8), the hottest month brings a real heat exclusion: hot, dry soil hurts germination and establishment, and the tops turn tough and sharply pungent, so sowing pauses in July and resumes in August. In the cooler Piedmont (zone 7), the spring harvest bridges naturally into the fall sowing with no real idle gap, so no heat exclusion is declared there. Sow a short row every two to three weeks through each window for a continuous supply.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Plant seed potato pieces per Virginia Cooperative Extension's zone 8 Potatoes table (Feb 20 to Apr 10); zone 7 runs about three weeks later (Mar 10 to May 20). VCE carries no fall column for potato; the belt's hot summer does not finish a fall crop.

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: New potatoes can be dug about 7 to 8 weeks in, but the main crop matures around 90 days from the earliest planting, the point tops begin to yellow.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The digging window closes around 120 days from the latest planting, as tops die back fully; tubers left in hot summer soil past this point lose quality.

plantings_provenance.basis: Built from VCE 426-331's zone 7/zone 8 Potatoes spring rows (no fall column; the belt's hot summer does not finish a fall crop). Harvest window derived from the crop's own days_to_maturity range (70 to 120 days) applied across the planting window's own span, matching the fast-to-slow digging convention used for this crop elsewhere.

8.zone_notes: Coastal Plain and Piedmont warm edge: plant seed potato pieces Feb 20 to Apr 10 as soon as the soil can be worked, hilling soil over the row as plants grow. Dig from late May through early August as tops yellow and die back; no fall crop, the belt's summer heat is past potato's comfort by then.

7.zone_notes: Piedmont: plant seed potato pieces Mar 10 to May 20, hilling soil over the row as plants grow. Dig from June through mid-September as tops yellow and die back; no fall crop follows.

potato.region_notes_beginner: In the Piedmont and Coastal Plain, grow potatoes once, in spring. Plant cut seed pieces as soon as the soil can be worked in late winter to spring, and mound soil over the row as plants grow so new potatoes stay covered. Dig new potatoes a couple of months in, and the main crop once the tops turn yellow and die down, from late spring into late summer. Skip a fall crop here; the summer heat that follows is past what potato likes.
potato.region_notes_seasoned: Potato in the Mid-Atlantic is a single spring crop: Virginia Cooperative Extension's 426-331 tables carry only a spring window (Feb 20 to Apr 10 in zone 8, Mar 10 to May 20 in zone 7), no fall column, honestly reflecting that the belt's hot, humid summer does not finish a second planting for this cool-season tuber, whose quality falls off in sustained heat above about 85°F. Plant seed pieces as soon as the soil can be worked, hill soil over the row as plants grow to keep developing tubers covered, and dig from late spring (zone 8) or early summer (zone 7) through late summer as tops yellow and die back.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.source_quote: Sow seeds indoors six to eight weeks before planting outside to get a head start on the growing season.
start_indoors.synthesis_note: UMN Extension recommends starting basil indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost date and transplanting after all frost risk has passed. 6-week lead (42 days) used as the primary offset, consistent with basil weeks_indoors=6.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote: Sow seeds directly into the ground after danger of spring frosts has passed.
plant_out.synthesis_note: Plant out after last frost once soil has warmed above 65°F, typically 1-2 weeks post-frost. Basil is frost-tender; no rushing. Applies to both transplants and direct sowing.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note: First harvest possible approximately 30 days after transplanting out (60-90 day DTM; pinching from top begins earlier at ~4 weeks). Leaf harvest can begin whenever plants have multiple true-leaf sets.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note: Basil is killed by first frost in cold zones. Harvest all remaining leaves before the first fall frost arrives. UMN: basil will not survive winter in the region.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note: Succession plantings: start new batches indoors every 3 weeks from the first start-indoors date through midsummer. Stop when a new transplant would not have 60+ days to harvest before first frost.

parsley.region_notes_seasoned: Parsley tolerates a light frost and, unlike its cool-season peers, does not heat-bolt, so the Piedmont and Coastal Plain grow it as one long continuous planting: soak the slow seed and direct sow about two weeks ahead of last frost (z7 Apr 15, z8 Apr 8), then cut cut-and-come-again through the humid summer and into fall, well past the first frost (z7 Oct 25, z8 Oct 30). No VCE or NC State planting table covers parsley; this window mirrors parsley's own existing northern_tier z7 structure (UMN Extension; Wisconsin Horticulture; Clemson), re-anchored to the mid_atlantic dates. Replace plants annually rather than overwintering them, since a second-year plant bolts and turns bitter.

In cold regions the clump dies back over winter and regrows in early spring; in mild and hot regions it holds through the cool season and slows or rests in extreme summer heat. One planting yields cut-and-come-again leaves for years, with the calendar pausing only where the summer is genuinely too hot for a cool-preferring plant. Windows are modeled from chives' cold-hardy, cool-season envelope and the regional planting-calendar sources. (UMN; Wisconsin Horticulture; MSU)

Plant one clump inside a pot or a buried, bottomless barrier a week or two after your last frost so it cannot take over the bed, then cut stems back by no more than a third whenever you harvest. This is a conservative estimate: there is no belt-specific extension guide for mint, so the window follows mint's own cold-hardier zone calendar shifted to this region's frost dates.
mint.region_notes_seasoned: Mint is a hardy, moisture-loving perennial set out as a division or rooted cutting, not seed, about a week after last frost (z7 Apr 15, z8 Apr 8); contain it in a pot or a buried barrier, since it spreads by runners. It returns each spring from its roots and crops through the Piedmont and Coastal Plain's humid summer into fall, with real winter dormancy after the first frost (z7 Oct 25, z8 Oct 30). No VCE or NC State planting table covers mint; this window mirrors mint's own existing northern_tier z7 structure (Utah State; Clemson; regional extension), re-anchored to the mid_atlantic dates. Pinch flower buds to keep the leaves tender and keep the soil evenly moist.

In cold-winter regions celery is grown as a single main crop: start seed indoors in late winter, transplant after the danger of hard frost and prolonged cold has passed (chilled young plants bolt), and grow through the relatively mild northern summer for a late-summer to fall harvest before hard freezes. Constant moisture and steady feeding through the long season are the limiting factors, not heat.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer heat gap (Jun, Jul, Aug) in the Piedmont and Coastal Plain: sustained temperatures above roughly 75°F fade viola blooms, stretch the plants, and end the cool-season show, and warm soil also inhibits germination, so no viola is grown through this stretch. Not a frost gap but a summer heat exclusion; bloom resumes as the weather cools, the same threshold documented for viola's cold-hardier zones. (Clemson HGIC; UF/IFAS)

viola.region_notes_beginner: Viola and pansy are the toughest cool-season flowers for the Piedmont and Coastal Plain, blooming right through frosty mornings: set out transplants in late winter to early spring, expect a pause through the hottest, most humid weeks of summer, then plant again in late summer for a fall show that runs well into November. This is a conservative estimate: there is no belt-specific extension guide for viola, so the window follows viola's own cold-hardier zone calendar shifted to this region's frost dates.
viola.region_notes_seasoned: Viola is exceptionally cold-hardy and blooms above freezing, so the Piedmont and Coastal Plain run it as a spring crop that can be started indoors and set out well ahead of the last frost (z7 Apr 15, z8 Apr 8), pausing through the region's hot, humid June to August stretch above roughly 75°F, then resuming from a September sowing that crops well past the first frost (z7 Oct 25, z8 Oct 30), on this frost-hardy flower's own tolerance. No VCE or NC State planting table covers viola; this window mirrors viola's own existing northern_tier z7 structure (Clemson HGIC; Penn State Extension; NC State Extension), re-anchored to the mid_atlantic dates. Deadhead through the season for a longer show.

bee-balm.region_notes_beginner: Bee balm is a hardy, pollinator-magnet perennial for the Piedmont and Coastal Plain: set out a transplant or spring division around your last frost, and it comes back every year, blooming mid to late summer for bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds. Give it full sun, good airflow, and even moisture to fend off powdery mildew. This is a conservative estimate: there is no belt-specific extension guide for bee balm, so the window follows bee balm's own cold-hardier zone calendar shifted to this region's frost dates.
bee-balm.region_notes_seasoned: Bee balm is planted once, around the last frost (z7 Apr 15, z8 Apr 8), and returns for years from its crown; it blooms mid to late summer, dies back with the first fall frost (z7 Oct 25, z8 Oct 30), and overwinters dormant. No VCE or NC State planting table covers bee balm; this window mirrors bee balm's own existing northern_tier z7 structure (NC State Extension), re-anchored to the mid_atlantic dates. The region's humid summers make powdery mildew the main pressure here, so site in full sun with generous spacing, keep soil evenly moist, and divide every 2 to 3 years for airflow.

transplant.synthesis_note_seasoned: Echinacea is established once from a spring division, transplant, or stratified seedling set out after hard frost, then grown as a hardy herbaceous perennial that returns from its crown each year. One planting yields for years; the calendar shows winter dormancy (cold_pause) where it freezes, spring regrowth, and a summer-into-fall bloom, with a single spring establishment plant token. (NC State; Clemson; regional extension)

echinacea.region_notes_beginner: Echinacea (purple coneflower) is a tough, long-lived perennial for the Piedmont and Coastal Plain: plant one division or transplant in spring after hard frost, and it comes back every year, blooming from summer into fall. Leave the last seed heads standing for goldfinches, then cut the stems back in late winter. This is a conservative estimate: there is no belt-specific extension guide for echinacea, so the window follows echinacea's own cold-hardier zone calendar shifted to this region's frost dates.
echinacea.region_notes_seasoned: Echinacea is planted once, in spring after hard frost (z7 Apr 15, z8 Apr 8), and returns for years from its crown; it blooms from summer into fall, dies back with the first fall frost (z7 Oct 25, z8 Oct 30), and overwinters dormant with no protection needed in this belt's climate. No VCE or NC State planting table covers echinacea; this window mirrors echinacea's own existing northern_tier z7 structure (NC State Extension; Penn State Extension), re-anchored to the mid_atlantic dates. Give it full sun and well-drained soil, and divide an established clump every 3 to 4 years.
